parts.title: Two computer programs working together: first outlining a worm's body, then sorting it, to find which body features predict how long a C. elegans worm lives and how much it moves
parts.abstract:
Abstract

The tiny roundworm C. elegans is a well-known "model organism": a living thing that scientists study closely to learn things that also apply to other animals, including humans. Researchers use it to study how genes and drugs affect aging, and many of these effects are shared with humans. It is also an important animal for basic research, and the study of diseases in C. elegans is a new field that is just starting.

In this work, we built a first working version of a computer system that uses a type of image-reading program called a convolutional neural network (CNN). The system does two jobs. First, it outlines the worm in a picture, a step called segmentation. Second, it picks out features of the worm's body that might help predict how long the worm will live. We used a collection of 734 worms that were followed from the start of their lives until they died, and we sorted them into long-lived and short-lived groups.

We designed a CNN called WormNet that predicts which group a worm belongs to from pictures of it as a young adult (between day 1 and day 3 of adulthood). We showed that WormNet, and also a well-known CNN called InceptionV3, can sort the worms into these groups successfully.

Next, we built HydraNet CNNs, based on a design called U-Net. HydraNet outlines the worm accurately and splits its body into three parts: the front (anterior), the middle (mid-body) and the back (posterior). We then combined three tools: HydraNet's body outlines, WormNet's predictions, and "class activation maps", which are heat maps showing which parts of a picture a CNN pays the most attention to when it makes a decision. Together, they let us find which body parts matter most for sorting worms by lifespan.

This two-step approach, first outlining the body and then sorting the worm, shows that the back part of the worm might be more important for telling long-lived worms apart. Our approach could help speed up the search for drugs that slow aging, and it could help researchers study diseases in C. elegans.

Keywords: aging, deep learning, Caenorhabditis elegans, machine learning that can be explained, convolutional neural networks
parts.introduction_first:
The roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) is a well-known model for studying ways to change the aging process. Using it, scientists have found many genes and drugs that affect aging. Some of the most promising anti-aging drugs are in two official lists of drugs that may be tested in people. Five of the 7 drugs on the top list (Tier 1) and 4 of the 6 on the second list (Tier 2) make C. elegans worms live longer. Many of the body processes that control aging are shared across different species, so we expect worms to be used a great deal, not only in research on long life but also in the new industry that is starting to sell anti-aging products [1]. On top of that, "humanized" worms, which carry human genes, are now being used to build promising models for neurodegeneration, the slow loss of nerve cells that happens in diseases such as Alzheimer's [2].

However, while the genes behind long life have been studied, the visible signs of aging in C. elegans are not yet well understood. In particular, we know little about the diseases that come with old age and how they develop. We also know little about which diseases decide how long a worm lives, and how they cause death [3]. Only recently have researchers described several such diseases, including a shrinking gut, tumors in the uterus and an infection of the pharynx, the worm's muscular throat [4–6]. For these reasons, finding new diseases in C. elegans, and especially finding out how they affect lifespan, is becoming an important challenge. Studying these diseases in worms might help us better understand aging, as well as how anti-aging drugs work and what effects they have.
parts.introduction_rest:
Recent progress in machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) [7] may help studies of aging in C. elegans. These computer methods can find and summarize patterns in behavior and body shape that nobody had noticed before, even in very large sets of experimental data.

Here are some examples. In one recent study, researchers measured several body processes in the same worms again and again over time. They then used a method called support vector regression, which fits a line or curve through data to predict a number. With it, they found that different features of the worms explained different amounts of the variation in how long the worms lived [8]. Movement explained 57% of that variation, cross-sectional size (how thick the worm is) 5%, texture 42%, autofluorescence (the natural glow of the worm's body) 52%, and the rate at which the worm lays eggs 28%.

Other studies have looked at how closely lifespan goes together with other features. Scientists measure this with a number called a correlation, written r. It runs from –1 to 1. A value near 1 means that when one thing goes up, the other tends to go up too. A value near –1 means that when one goes up, the other tends to go down. A value near 0 means there is little link. Interestingly, the number of young a worm produces (its brood size) was linked to its lifespan in mated hermaphrodites, worms that carry both male and female parts (r = 0.28) [9].

Independent studies also confirm that how the muscles work is probably the body feature that best predicts lifespan [10]. Two measures of the pharynx, the worm's muscular throat, were strongly linked to how long the worms lived. One was the span of fast pumping of the pharynx (r = 0.49), and the other was the span of pharynx pumping (r = 0.83).

Speed also predicts lifespan. The top speed a worm reaches on day 9 [11] explains 71% of the variation in lifespan, and how quickly the worm slows down between days 3 and 9 [12] explains 91%.

Researchers have also found features at the level of cells and molecules that predict how long C. elegans lives. When young adults on day 1 were given a heat shock, the gene hsp-16.2 was switched on. How strongly it was switched on was linked to lifespan [13]. Another gene, sod-3, is normally active all the time. Its normal level on day 9 was also linked to lifespan (r = 0.57), and this probably reflects the worm's response to food that is harmful to it [14]. The activity of a gene called mir-71 from day 4 onwards can be very predictive, explaining 47% of the variation in lifespan [15].

One result is especially striking. The size of the nucleolus, a small structure inside the cell's nucleus, was measured on day 1. Worms with a larger nucleolus tended to live much shorter lives (r = –0.93). This points to protein-making that is out of control as an important part of aging [16].

It is also worth noting that, early on, researchers used a computer vision approach to sort C. elegans into different aging types. They used a method called a linear discriminant classifier, which separates groups by looking at a few key measurements. With it, they sorted pictures of pharynxes from worms of different ages, so that the worms could then be studied at the molecular level [17].

Among the many machine learning methods, one of the most powerful, especially for pictures, is the convolutional neural network (CNN) [18]. CNNs are inspired by the way the visual cortex, the part of the brain that handles sight, is built. CNNs have achieved impressive results in recognizing pictures. On MNIST, a collection of pictures of handwritten digits, they perform almost as well as people. In recognizing traffic signs, they did twice as well as people [19]. CNNs have also won "The ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge" again and again, a competition for sorting pictures into categories [20, 21].

Adding "skipped connections" to CNNs, which let information skip past some of the program's layers, made them much faster and more accurate. CNNs with these connections, called residual CNNs, are now the best available for sorting pictures [22, 23]. Some residual networks are built as an "encoder" that shrinks a picture down and a "decoder" that builds it back up, such as U-Net [24], V-Net and Tiramisu. These also do better than the older methods used in medical imaging to outline objects in pictures, such as tracing edges, setting brightness cut-offs and drawing regions [25].

Despite these impressive results, deep learning has one main weakness. These programs are "black boxes": it is hard to find out which features of a picture led the program to its decision [26]. To get around this, researchers have proposed several "saliency" methods, which show which parts of a picture matter most [27–29]. One such method uses a part of the program called the global average pooling layer to produce a class activation map. This map shows which regions of the picture belong to each category, without anyone having to teach the program where to look [30]. These general-purpose maps of where the program pays attention can help researchers understand how CNNs tell things apart. However, so far, no one has developed a way to combine two kinds of maps: body outlines that make biological sense, and saliency maps that show what a program uses to sort things. Such a combination could help researchers discover new visible signs of aging by understanding the program's decisions.

Remarkably, CNNs have recently been used to predict how long worms live. In the first study, researchers used a set of 913 pictures of C. elegans. Each day had at least 30 worms, and all of them were put to sleep before being photographed. A program built on a design called InceptionResNetV2 predicted each worm's age. When it predicted a number, its average error (the mean absolute error, or MAE) was 0.96 days. When it sorted worms into age groups, it was right 57.6% of the time [31].

In another study, the researchers used an automatic camera system that could follow the same worm for its whole life. This gave them data on 734 worms, with a picture taken every 3.5 hours. They used U-Net to outline the worms against the background. Then they measured the positions of points along each worm's body and used them to draw the worm as a straight line. After that, they used a changed version of a program called ResNet34 to predict each worm's age from the raw pictures, with an average error of just 0.6 days [32].

In this work, we used the same set of pictures as in [8, 32]. Instead of predicting each worm's age, we built a CNN-based system that we call WormNet. It sorts young adults (day 1 to day 3) into short-lived and long-lived groups. We also designed a way to find the features that matter most for this sorting.

In the same way, we used WormNet to sort C. elegans by how it moves. To understand the sorting results in a planned way, we paired the sorting CNN with a second CNN that outlines the worm. For this, we designed a new program based on U-Net, called HydraNet. HydraNet outlines the worm against the background and also splits the worm's body into the front, middle and back parts.

To understand the sorting results, we combined HydraNet's body outlines with class activation maps made by WormNet. Looking at these maps together with the body outlines in this two-step way let us find the features that are responsible for predicting lifespan. Finally, we checked our results on higher-resolution versions of the worm pictures, with the worms outlined. For this check, we used a residual CNN called InceptionV3, which can capture more detail, together with our own careful interpretation of the results.
parts.methods:
## Materials and methods

### How we wrote the computer programs

We wrote all of our computer code in the Python programming language, version 3.6. To run our neural networks, we used two widely used software packages: TensorFlow, in version 1.9.0 or 2.3.0 [37], and Keras, in version 2.2.2 [38]. Neural networks work with large grids of numbers, and we prepared and handled these grids with a tool called Numpy, version 1.15.0 [39]. We kept our Python setup running with a package manager called Anaconda. Anyone can find our code on GitHub, a website where people share code (https://github.com/ails-institute/DeepLongevity).

### Training the programs

A neural network learns by being shown many examples and then adjusting itself a little each time it makes a mistake. This is called training. We trained WormNet and fine-tuned InceptionV3 on an ordinary desktop computer. It had an Intel Core i7-8700K processor running at 3.7 GHz, 32 GB of memory (RAM), and a powerful graphics card (GPU), the GeForce 1080 Ti. We trained U-Net and HydraNet on a remote computer with a GPU (for example, an NVIDIA Tesla V100) through Google Colaboratory, an online service that gives researchers access to such computers. We also used Google Colaboratory to run the programs on new pictures and to analyze the results.

### Settings we chose for the programs

Before a neural network starts learning, we have to choose some settings. These are called hyperparameters. They include the learning rate, which controls how big a step the network takes each time it corrects itself. They also include settings for the optimizer, the method that makes those corrections. For WormNet, we used a method called Adam. We started it with a learning rate of 0.005 and its standard settings: beta 1 of 0.9, beta 2 of 0.999, epsilon of 1e-08, and decay of 0.

To help the network learn, we used a loss function. This is a score that measures how wrong the network's answers are, and the network tries to make this score as small as possible. For WormNet, the score was called binary cross-entropy. It suits a task with two possible answers, here long-lived or short-lived.

We also used data augmentation. This means we made extra training pictures by changing the originals slightly, for example by flipping or rotating them. We made 30 of these changed copies for each epoch, which is one full pass through all the training pictures.

We trained U-Net and HydraNet with the Adam optimizer as well, starting with a learning rate of 0.001 and using the default settings. For their job of outlining the worm and splitting it into body parts, we used a score called Dice loss (see https://github.com/ails-institute/DeepLongevity). It measures how well the network's outline matches the correct one.

### How we compared the groups

To check whether the groups of worms differed, we used a statistical test called a one-way ANOVA. It compares the average values of several groups at once. We followed it with Tukey's HSD correction, which makes the test stricter so that we are less likely to find a difference just by chance when we make many comparisons. We ran these tests in a program called GraphPad Prism.

### Designing the programs and choosing their settings

We wanted U-Net, WormNet, HydraNet and InceptionV3 to work as well as possible. So we adjusted their settings by trial and error, based on what worked well in practice. These settings included, among others, the learning rate and the dropout coefficient. Dropout is a way of stopping the network from leaning too heavily on any one part of itself, and the coefficient controls how strongly it does this.

For the basic comparison, we kept the settings of similar programs as close to each other as possible. For the new programs, we started with the smallest design that could still do the job. We then made the design bigger and more complex step by step, until the results stopped improving.

### The pictures of the worms

We have placed the original pictures in a public online store for images, the BioImage Archive (EMBL): https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biostudies/studies/S-BIAD300.
parts.results:
## Results

We built our first working version of the system using time-lapse pictures of 734 C. elegans worms, filmed from the first day of adulthood until each worm died [8, 15]. To make the computer understand these pictures automatically, we needed to solve two problems. The first was outlining the worm against its background. The second was telling apart the different parts of the worm's body (Figure 1).

To do this, we marked 130 pictures of adult worms by hand. For each picture we drew a mask, which is a black-and-white outline, for the front, the middle and the back of the worm. Adding the three masks together gave one mask for the whole worm (Figure 1F–1H). We then split these pictures into two groups. The training group (90 pictures) is used to teach the program. The test group (40 pictures) is kept aside to check how well the program works on pictures it has never seen. We split the groups by the ID number of each worm, so that no worm's features could leak from the training group into the test group.

We started with the simpler problem of outlining the whole worm. For this we built a fairly simple design, similar to U-Net [24]. A U-Net has two halves. The first half, called the encoder, shrinks the picture step by step to pick out its main features. The second half, called the decoder, builds the picture back up. At the end, a small extra part called a sigmoid head gives a yes-or-no answer for each pixel: worm or not worm. Figure 1A shows the encoder and decoder as the left part (α) and the right part (β) of the design. To save computing time, we shrank the raw pictures to 96 × 96 pixels.

To measure how good the outlines were, we used a score called the Jaccard index. It compares the area where the program's outline and the hand-drawn outline agree with the total area they cover together. A score of 1 would be a perfect match. While training, we used a measure called the Dice loss, which tells the program how far its outlines are from the correct ones, so it can correct itself. On this fairly simple task, the Jaccard index reached 0.97 on both the training and the test groups (Figure 1A, 1B; Materials and Methods gives the detailed settings).

Next, we wanted to outline each body part separately. We turned the problem into a "multi-class" one, where the program has to choose between several labels at once: front, middle, back or whole worm. Each mask was written as a list of yes-or-no labels, one for each part, a format called one-hot encoding. We used a U-Net-like design again (Figure 1C, 1I). As we expected, sorting into several groups is harder than sorting into two. The Jaccard index dropped to 0.92 on the training group and 0.91 on the test group. This suggests mild overfitting, which means the program learned the training pictures a little too closely and did slightly worse on new ones.

**Figure 1.** How we worked out a way to outline the worm's body parts. (A) The U-Net design taken from [24]. On the left is a microscope picture of C. elegans taken with light shining through the worm. The area shown is 580.5 μm by 580.5 μm, shrunken to 96 × 96 pixels. On the right is a yes-or-no outline mask as the output. The numbers show how many filters (small pattern detectors) each layer has: convolutional (Conv), batch normalization (BN) and activation (Act) layers. Max pooling layers were combined with spatial dropout (SDO). Arrows show skip connections: a layer from the encoder is joined (Concat) to a layer from the decoder (Transp, a layer that expands the picture back to its size) to make a new layer. For the drawing, the design is split into a left part (α) and a right part (β). (B) The U-Net design for yes-or-no outlines. (C) The U-Net design for several labels. (D) The HydraNet 3 design. (E) The HydraNet 4 design. In B–E, α is the left part and β is the right part of the design in (A). The graphs below show how well each design outlined the worms, measured as Jaccard index, during each round of training (each epoch). (F) An example picture from the test group. (G) The hand-drawn outlines of the worm's body parts. (H) The yes-or-no U-Net's output on a test picture. (I) The multi-class U-Net's output on a test picture. Here the red and blue masks overlap, so the front and back parts look magenta. (J) HydraNet 3's output on a test picture. (K) HydraNet 4's output on a test picture.

One thing the multi-class U-Net did poorly was telling the front and back of the worm apart, so its masks for these two parts overlapped (Figure 1I). To get around this, we designed a new design using the left (α) and right (β) parts of U-Net. Instead of one β part, we gave the design several β parts, each solving its own yes-or-no outlining problem (Figure 1D, 1E). We called this design HydraNet. All the β parts share the same input layers, and each has its own layers for one body part. This lets the design learn everything from the picture to the outline in one go, while each part still solves a simpler yes-or-no problem.

HydraNet3 had 3 β parts, one each for the front, middle and back of the worm. HydraNet4 had 4 β parts, for the front, middle, back and the whole worm. To see how well HydraNet worked overall, we measured the Jaccard index for each β part separately and then took the average. Remarkably, both HydraNet3 and HydraNet4 reached an average Jaccard index of 0.97 on both the training and the test groups. This shows they generalize well, meaning they work on new pictures too (Figure 1D, 1E, 1J, 1K). HydraNet4 also reached this level of performance earlier in training than HydraNet3 (Figure 1D, 1E insets). This suggests that adding a more general label, the whole worm, may help.

Next, we wanted programs that could sort worms by how much they move and by how long they live. We split all 734 worms into two movement groups: low and high. A worm counted as high movement if it crawled farther in total over its life than the average worm, and low movement if it crawled less. We also split them into two lifespan groups: "short-lived" worms that lived 7 days or less, and "long-lived" worms that lived 8 days or more. The task was to predict which group a worm belongs to from pictures taken on day 1, day 2 or day 3.

Our collection of pictures is fairly small. A very complex design could overfit on it, so we built a fairly simple CNN that we called WormNet. It had 5 convolutional layers, each followed by a max pooling layer, which shrinks the picture by keeping only the strongest signal in each small patch. To help the program generalize, we added dropout and batch normalization to each convolutional layer. Dropout randomly switches off some parts of the network during training, so the network cannot lean too heavily on any one of them. Batch normalization keeps the numbers flowing through the network in a steady range.

The last max pooling layer was flattened into one long list of numbers. This was connected to a fully connected layer, which links every number to every other, and then to a softmax layer, which turns the results into chances for each group. We used binary cross-entropy as the loss, a measure of how wrong the program's guesses are. All the layers except the last one used a simple rule called a rectified linear unit (ReLU) to decide how strongly each part should respond (Figure 2A; Materials and Methods gives the detailed settings). We used WormNet to sort worms by both movement and lifespan (Figures 2 and 3).

To reduce overfitting further, we made 30 extra versions of each picture using Keras image generators, a tool that changes pictures at random. Each picture was flipped left-to-right and top-to-bottom at random, shifted sideways and up-and-down by up to 10%, and turned by a random angle up to 90 degrees. The empty areas left by these changes were filled in with the nearest value.

**Figure 2.** Sorting worms by movement from microscope pictures taken at the end of their lives, with an explanation of the program's choices based on body outlines and heat maps. (A) The WormNet design. The numbers show how many filters each layer has: convolutional (Conv), fully connected (FC), batch normalization (BN) and activation (Act) layers. Max pooling layers were combined with spatial dropout (SDO). (B–D) For pictures taken on day 1, day 2 and day 3, the training loss (cost function), accuracy, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and confusion matrix. Black lines show the training group and light-grey lines show the test (validation) group. (E) A test picture of a low-movement worm. (F) The top quarter of the heat map (class activation map, CAM) for the picture in E, together with the share of the heat map that falls on each body part, measured with HydraNet 4 and the body outlines (percent overlap). One-way ANOVA with Tukey's HSD correction. Mean ± SEM, p-value <0.0001. (G) A test picture of a high-movement worm. (H) The top quarter of the heat map (CAM) for the picture in G, together with the share of the heat map that falls on each body part, measured with HydraNet 4 and the body outlines (percent overlap). One-way ANOVA with Tukey's HSD correction. Mean ± SEM, p-value <0.0001. The area shown is 580.5 μm by 580.5 μm.

**Figure 3.** Sorting worms by lifespan from microscope pictures taken at the end of their lives, with an explanation of the program's choices based on body outlines and heat maps. (A–C) For pictures taken on day 1, day 2 and day 3, the training loss (cost function), accuracy, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and confusion matrix. Black lines show the training group and light-grey lines show the test (validation) group. (D) A test picture of a short-lived worm. (E) The top quarter of the heat map (CAM) for the picture in D, together with the share of the heat map that falls on each body part, measured with HydraNet 4 and the body outlines (percent overlap). One-way ANOVA with Tukey's HSD correction. Mean ± SEM, ***p-value <0.001, ****p-value <0.0001. (F) A test picture of a long-lived worm. (G) The top quarter of the heat map (CAM) for the picture in F, together with the share of the heat map that falls on each body part, measured with HydraNet 4 and the body outlines (percent overlap). One-way ANOVA with Tukey's HSD correction. Mean ± SEM, *p-value <0.05, **p-value <0.01. The area shown is 580.5 μm by 580.5 μm.

WormNet sorted worms by total movement well. On the test pictures of day 3 adults, it was right 88% of the time (accuracy 0.88). Its precision was 0.86 and its recall was 0.86. Precision is the share of worms it called "low movement" that really were low movement, and recall is the share of all low-movement worms that it found. We also measured the area under the ROC curve (AUC ROC). This score runs from 0.5, which is no better than guessing, to 1, which is perfect. For day 3 it was 0.56. On day 1 and day 2 pictures, WormNet did slightly worse (Figure 2B–2D), with AUC ROC scores of 0.51 and 0.55.

We wanted to be sure that WormNet's predictions came mostly from the worm's body and not from its surroundings. So we made a set of artificial background pictures, in which we had removed the worm using the outlines. To stop the worm's outline from affecting training, we filled the empty pixels with random noise (Supplementary Figure 1). Our results suggested that WormNet's performance comes mainly from the worm's body rather than from the background.

To find out which body part might guide WormNet's decisions, we used our two-step approach: first outlining the body, then sorting the worm. We made heat maps (class activation maps, or CAMs) for a low-movement worm (Figure 2E, 2F) and a high-movement worm (Figure 2G, 2H). Next, we outlined each picture with HydraNet4. We then took the top quarter of the heat map and combined it with HydraNet4's body outlines. For each worm, we worked out what percentage of the heat map fell on each body part, for both the high- and low-movement worms.

To check whether this explanation was statistically significant, we used a test called one-way ANOVA with Tukey's honest significant difference (HSD) correction (Figure 2F for low-movement worms, Figure 2H for high-movement worms). ANOVA compares the averages of several groups, and Tukey's correction adjusts for making many comparisons at once. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. For p < 0.05, that means less than 5% of the time.

The test suggested that, for both low- and high-movement worms, the front part of the worm was covered by the heat map significantly less (31%) than the middle (34%) and the back (34%). There was no significant difference between the middle and the back.

Next, we used WormNet to sort worms into long-lived and short-lived groups. As with movement, WormNet did best on day 3 adults. On the test pictures, it was right 72% of the time (accuracy 0.72), with precision 0.73, recall 0.71 and AUC ROC 0.61. On day 2 and day 1 pictures, its AUC ROC scores were lower, at 0.53 and 0.52. The confusion matrix, a table showing which groups the program mixed up, suggested that the CNN did worse at sorting short-lived worms (Figure 3A–3C).

We then explained the program's choices using HydraNet4 and WormNet together, followed by the one-way ANOVA test. For lifespan, the explanation suggested that the front part of the worm was significantly less prominent in the heat maps (32%) than the middle and the back (Figure 3D, 3E for short-lived worms, Figure 3F, 3G for long-lived worms). This difference was less significant for long-lived worms than for short-lived worms. There was no significant difference between the middle and the back.

To check these findings in a separate way, we trained another lifespan program, this time using a well-known CNN called InceptionV3 [33], and explained its choices by hand (Figure 4). This time we wanted sharper heat maps, so instead of shrinking the pictures to 96 × 96 pixels, we used the full 900 × 900 pictures, cropped to 800 × 800 pixels (516 × 516 μm). InceptionV3 is a much more powerful CNN, so it was likely to overfit on our fairly small collection of pictures (Figure 4C, 4D). To prevent this, we used early stopping: we stopped training once the program stopped improving. We also outlined the worms and removed the background, so that InceptionV3 saw only the part of the picture that mattered.

InceptionV3 did about as well as WormNet, reaching 70% accuracy on the test pictures for lifespan (Figure 4A). Just as with the HydraNet4-WormNet approach, the hand-made explanation showed that InceptionV3's heat maps highlighted the front of the worm less often. Importantly, though, because the pictures were sharper, the heat maps now pinned down the body parts much better. This let us name a body part as a possible deciding feature in each case (Figure 4B). Interestingly, the body parts highlighted by the heat maps show that the back of the worm matters more for sorting long-lived worms. This suggests that the features that predict long life could be found in the back part of the worm's body.

**Figure 4.** Heat maps (class activation maps, CAMs) from the InceptionV3 network, trained on sharp pictures, that point to body regions linked to lifespan. (A) Examples of heat maps pointing to the front (left) or the back (right) of a worm. Here, an area of 516 by 516 μm was shown in an 800 × 800 pixel picture, giving sharper input. (B) How important each body part is for the program's prediction, measured as the percentage of heat maps that highlight that body part. (C–D) Training loss and accuracy for the InceptionV3 network.
parts.discussion:
## Discussion

C. elegans is a classic model for studying aging, and more than 4000 papers have been published on it so far. Robots have also made progress. Even so, measuring how long a C. elegans worm lives is still done by hand and takes a lot of work. New methods are starting to appear. One is the lifespan machine, which uses flatbed scanners to check at the same time whether a large number of worms on a plate are still alive [34]. Another is Worm corals, an automatic way of raising worms that lets researchers follow each worm through its whole life and measure it in much more detail [8].

The detailed body measurements from Worm corals showed that three things best predict how long a worm will live: how much it moves, its autofluorescence (the natural glow of some of its body parts) and how much its body texture breaks down. However, it is still unclear which exact body features reflect disease and decide how long a worm lives. Researchers also found that body measurements taken before day 3 or 4 of adulthood, and single biomarkers labelled with GFP (a green glowing protein that scientists attach to particular body parts), cannot tell short-lived worms from long-lived ones [8, 15]. Predictions based on the nucleolus, a small structure inside the cell's nucleus, were made on day 1 adults. Those predictions used worms that had been fixed, meaning preserved so they no longer move, and looked at them at 100 times magnification. No automatic screening system can do this.

In this work, we used the collection of worms made by the Pincus lab [8, 15]. We showed that our newly designed WormNet could successfully tell short-lived worms from long-lived ones, even from pictures taken on day 1 or day 2. Importantly, WormNet did best on day 3 (Figure 2A–2C). It was even better at sorting worms that moved a lot from worms that moved very little, reaching 88% accuracy on day 1 adults (Figure 3). We expect that collecting more data and improving the design of the CNN could make WormNet work even better. This would reduce two problems. The first is overfitting, when a program learns the quirks of its training pictures too closely and then does worse on new ones. The second is bias, when a program leans towards one answer more than it should.

CNNs have been used before to predict C. elegans lifespan, both by giving a number (regression) and by sorting worms into groups (classification) [31]. In that work, people sorted the worms by hand into curvy and straight postures, which made the predictions more accurate. Even so, the accuracy stayed fairly low, because there were only 913 pictures.

The Pincus lab's collection of worms was also used to test how well CNNs can predict lifespan [32]. As we mentioned earlier, the researchers outlined the worms and turned them into straightened versions, which were then used to train the CNN [32]. Having more pictures helped the program predict the worms' age as a number. Interestingly, the researchers found that the worm's outline alone holds only a little information for estimating age. Information from the background, however, can greatly improve accuracy, though this value comes from the conditions of the experiment rather than from the worm itself. So it is possible that part of the accuracy of WormNet in our tests comes from the background. However, our experiments suggest (Supplementary Figure 1) that WormNet's performance depends mostly on the shape and features of the C. elegans body, not on the background of the pictures. Importantly, the program in [32] was first trained on worm pictures that had been turned into body-coordinate maps, which are pictures where each point is labelled by its position on the worm's body. This training made it more accurate on ordinary pictures, which suggests that the worm's organs and texture are useful for predicting age.

Besides sorting young adults by lifespan or movement, we also wanted to find which features matter most for the prediction. As a first test, we asked which body part, the front, the middle or the back, holds the features that most affect how long a worm lives. We designed HydraNet 3 and 4, new designs based on U-Net, and showed that they can successfully outline the worm's body parts. They reached a perfect Jaccard index, a score that measures how well an outline matches the real body part, where 1 is a perfect match.

Importantly, we wanted a way to explain the program's decisions that is built into the design from the start. To do this, we used two kinds of sorting that make biological sense: sorting by lifespan and sorting by movement. These gave us heat maps (class activation maps) showing which parts of the picture mattered most [30, 35]. We combined them with HydraNet's body outlines, which split the worm into the front, middle and back, to find which body part is useful for the sorting. In addition, although less detailed, the results from this two-step approach agreed with a separate program that was trained on its own. This program was a yes-or-no classifier based on the InceptionV3 CNN. It was trained on full-resolution pictures of 800 × 800 pixels, with the worms cut out from their background. It gave results similar to WormNet's, but it generalizes less well, because it overfits more (Figure 4). With InceptionV3, though, the heat maps could point to particular body parts, and our analysis suggests that features in the back part of the worm might be more important for sorting long-lived worms.

This approach opens a path to finding new important age biomarkers in C. elegans automatically, given a big increase in picture resolution and the use of body-coordinate maps. HydraNets could outline organs that are not labelled, such as the pharynx, or body parts labelled with GFP. Their ability to predict lifespan could then be tested with the heat maps and with WormNet. It is tempting to speculate that, like generative adversarial networks [36], future versions of this two-step approach, first outlining the body and then sorting the worm, could be trained end-to-end, meaning all the steps learn together from start to finish, and could be used for everyday scientific discovery.

This first working version of an automatic analysis system will be useful for finding aging biomarkers without harming the worms, especially in young C. elegans adults on days 1 to 3. It has great potential to speed up the testing of drugs for slowing aging. Developing this method will also help researchers find and describe new diseases in C. elegans that matter for basic aging research. So that other researchers can use it, we have shared our code on GitHub (https://github.com/ails-institute/DeepLongevity).
